prf:algebraic-gns-embedding:
Proof Proof of the Markov-trace GNS embedding. Four standard components are assembled.

Tower of inclusions. The Hecke algebra H_n(R, q) has presentation by braid generators \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_{n-1} modulo the braid relations and the quadratic relation \sigma_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1. The inclusion H_n(q) \hookrightarrow H_{n+1}(q) adjoins \sigma_n. This inclusion is unital, R-linear, and commutes with the *-structure \sigma_i^* = \sigma_i. (This is the *-structure for which positivity below holds; it is distinct from the bar involution \sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_i^{-1}, q \mapsto q^{-1}, which does not fix z = q^3/(q^2+1).) The sequence \{H_n(q)\}_{n \geq 1} forms a filtered inductive system of unital *-algebras over R, with colimit H_\infty(q) = \bigcup_n H_n(q) [jones1985].

Markov property. The Markov trace \mathrm{tr}_{M,n} \colon H_n(q) \to R satisfies the recursion \mathrm{tr}_{M,n+1}(x \cdot \sigma_n) = z \cdot \mathrm{tr}_{M,n}(x) for any x \in H_n(q), where z = q^3/(q^2+1) (Jones–Markov trace). Equivalently, \mathrm{tr}_{M,n+1}|_{H_n(q)} = \mathrm{tr}_{M,n}. This compatibility with the inclusions defines a unique R\otimes\mathbb{Q}-linear trace \mathrm{tr}_M \colon H_\infty(q) \to R\otimes\mathbb{Q} extending all \mathrm{tr}_{M,n} by the universal property of the colimit.

Positivity. Let q > 0 be real. At z = q^3/(q^2+1) the Markov trace vanishes on every Wedderburn block with three or more rows, so it factors through the Temperley–Lieb quotient \mathrm{TL}_n(\delta) with loop value \delta = [2]_q = q + q^{-1}. Jones proved that the Markov trace on \mathrm{TL}_n(\delta) is a positive functional, \mathrm{tr}_{M,n}(x^* x) \geq 0, whenever \delta \geq 2 [jones1985]. Here q + q^{-1} \geq 2 for every real q > 0, with equality only at q = 1. So \mathrm{tr}_M is a positive trace on H_\infty(q) for every real q > 0, and in particular at q_0. There is no threshold in q to be near.

In Wedderburn terms, \mathrm{tr}_{M,n} = \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \chi^\lambda, and on each block the trace is y_\lambda times the matrix trace in Wenzl's orthogonal (seminormal) representation, where each \sigma_i acts by a real symmetric matrix [wenzl1988]. Positivity is then y_\lambda \geq 0 for every \lambda. The closed-form Ocneanu weight at z = q^3/(q^2+1) is strictly positive on every shape with at most two rows, for q > 0, q \neq 1, and zero on the rest. That this closed form is the Markov weight at general n is the classical Ocneanu–Wenzl formula; it is proved here only at n = 3 and checked numerically through n = 6, so the positivity statement supports the cited result and does not replace it.

GNS construction. Define the left ideal \mathcal{N} := \{x \in H_\infty(q) : \mathrm{tr}_M(x^* x) = 0\}. At z = q^3/(q^2+1) this ideal is not trivial: \mathrm{tr}_M = \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \chi^\lambda with y_\lambda = 0 precisely when \ell(\lambda) \geq 3, so \mathcal{N} is the sum of those Wedderburn blocks — the Temperley–Lieb radical — and the GNS quotient is H_\infty(q)/\mathrm{rad} \cong \mathrm{TL}_\infty(q), not H_\infty(q) itself. Positivity and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |\mathrm{tr}_M(x^* y)|^2 \leq \mathrm{tr}_M(x^* x)\,\mathrm{tr}_M(y^* y) guarantee \mathcal{N} is a well-defined ideal. The quotient V := H_\infty(q) / \mathcal{N} forms an H_\infty(q)-module under left multiplication. The bilinear form \langle [x], [y] \rangle := \mathrm{tr}_M(x^* y) is sesquilinear and positive definite on V. Its completion \mathcal{H} is a separable Hilbert space. Separability follows because H_\infty(q) admits a countable basis as an R\otimes\mathbb{Q}-module.

The left-multiplication action \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(a)[x] := [a x] extends to a bounded operator on \mathcal{H}. The trace Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields the bound \|\pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(a)\| \leq \|a\|_2. The representation is faithful: \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(a) = 0 implies \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(a)[1] = [a] = 0, requiring a \in \mathcal{N}, which means \mathrm{tr}_M(a^* a) = 0, and thus a = 0 in the trace-quotient. The *-property \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(a^*) = \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(a)^* holds on the dense subspace V \subset \mathcal{H} and extends to \mathcal{H} by continuity. \square
rem:algebraic-gns-embedding-interpretati: Remark The GNS image as a type II_1 subfactor. The image M := \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(H_\infty(q))'' forms a finite type II_1 von Neumann algebra. This realizes the Jones–Wenzl subfactor planar algebra. The subfactor theory machinery applies directly to the QOU algebraic data.
rem:algebraic-gns-embedding-cfs-conseque: Remark Consequence for the \mu_{\mathrm{arch}} programme: the operator-algebra carrier is in hand; only the CFS identification is conjectural. Consequence for the \mu_{\mathrm{arch}} programme. The operator-algebra realisation of the QOU pre-Archimedean aether derives from the Jones–Wenzl theorem (Markov-trace GNS embedding). The exact CFS Lagrangian form remains open.
rem:non-commutative-probability-dictiona:
Remark QOU as a non-commutative probability space: transfer matrices, traces, knot invariants as moments. The Hecke-algebra GNS data (algebraic GNS embedding) provides a non-commutative probability space [biane1998].

The dictionary.

See Table.

Three structural consequences.

  1. Knot theory evaluates non-commutative moments. Closed-braid knot invariants evaluate joint transfer matrix moments under \mathrm{tr}_M. The Kashaev–Murakami–Murakami volume conjecture operates as a free-entropy log-asymptotic.
  2. Wedderburn idempotents define events. The central projectors e_\lambda partition the unit. The Plancherel measure w_\lambda(q) = \mathrm{tr}_M(e_\lambda) assigns probability mass.
  3. Jucys--Murphy elements are commuting random variables. Biane proved large-n J_k elements converge to semicircle distributions at q = 1 [biane1998]. The q-deformed version (Féray--Méliot) yields a q-Gaussian [marsh2006].

Formal equivalence. The Hecke algebra under the Markov trace operates as a (W^*, \mathrm{tr}) probability space.

Imported tools. Voiculescu's R-/S-transforms, Speicher's free cumulants, free entropy, and Biane's asymptotic representation theory.

prop:q-plancherel-asymptotic-skeleton:
Proposition Asymptotic skeleton of the q-Plancherel measure \mathbb{M}_{n,q} — convergence on a continuous Young-diagram space. Let \mathbb{M}_{n,q} denote the q-Plancherel measure on partitions of n,

  \mathbb{M}_{n,q}(\lambda)
  \;=\; \frac{q^{n(\lambda)}\, f^\lambda}
             {\prod_{\square \in \lambda} \{h(\square)\}_q},
  \qquad
  \{k\}_q \;=\; \frac{q^k - 1}{q - 1},
  \quad
  n(\lambda) \;=\; \sum_i (i-1)\lambda_i ,

with f^\lambda the number of standard Young tableaux and h(\square) the hook lengths. Here n(\lambda) is Macdonald's partition statistic, not a function of the size n — the two are distinct objects sharing a glyph, and the size is always the bare n. Write \lambda' for the conjugate (transposed) partition and c(\square) = j - i for the content of the box in row i, column j. The blackboard-bold \mathbb{M} follows the \mathbb{V} precedent in the notation register: it is the source literature's own symbol, raised out of plain M and \mathcal{M}, both of which are claimed here (the latter by the mass endomorphism). Define a topological space \mathcal{K}_q (the q-deformed Kerov limit-shape space) and pushforward maps

  \iota_n \colon \{\lambda \vdash n\}
    \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{K}_q,
  \qquad
  n \in \mathbb{N},

such that \mu_n^{(q)} := (\iota_n)_*\,\mathbb{M}_{n,q} satisfy:

  1. (Existence at q = 1.) The sequence \{\mu_n^{(1)}\} converges weakly to \mu_\infty^{(1)} [vershik-kerov1977, biane1998].
  2. (Asymptotics at generic q.) The row lengths obey a law of large numbers, \lambda_i/n \to (1-q)q^{i-1} in probability, and their fluctuations are asymptotically Gaussian at scale \sqrt{n} [feray-meliot2012].
  3. (Limit identification, conjectural.) For q \neq 1, \{\mu_n^{(q)}\} converges weakly to \mu_\infty^{(q)}. Identify \mu_\infty^{(q)} with a measure on \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(H_\infty(q)).

Which weight this is, and why it changed

Identification of \mathbb{M}_{n,q} with the Molien fake-degree measure. Note that the Plancherel measure \mathbb{M}_{n,q} governing clause 2 is distinct from the squared-quantum-dimension weight w_\lambda^{(n)}(q) = \dim_q^2(\lambda)/[n]_q!; rather, \mathbb{M}_{n,q} coincides with the Molien fake-degree weight, which satisfies

  \frac{f^\lambda \, q^{-\kappa_\lambda} \, \dim_q(\lambda)}{[n]_q!}
  \;=\; \mathbb{M}_{n,\,q^2}(\lambda),
  \qquad
  \kappa_\lambda \;=\; \sum_{\square \in \lambda} c(\square),

verified in exact rational arithmetic for every partition of n = 1,\dots,9. So this proposition is not being restated over a new object; it is being restated over one the corpus has had all along, with the substitution Q = q^2 making the identification.

The exponent \kappa_\lambda is forced, not chosen. Substituting Q = q^2 into the display above leaves q^{2n(\lambda) - \sum_\square h(\square) + n}, which collapses to q^{-\kappa_\lambda} by two identities — \sum_\square h(\square) = n(\lambda) + n(\lambda') + n and \kappa_\lambda = n(\lambda') - n(\lambda) — each verified independently over all partitions of n \leq 10 in the same probe. Without them the identity would be an agreement at 96 sample points; with them it is a derivation.

This also explains a coincidence the corpus carried without comment: the proved identity \sum_\lambda f^\lambda q^{-\kappa_\lambda}\dim_q(\lambda) = [n]_q! holds for every n, and \mathbb{M}_{n,q} is a probability measure by construction. Those are the same theorem.

The aether sits at q > 1, and that costs an orientation, not the theorem

[feray-meliot2012] states its asymptotics for q < 1, while the aether gives Q = q_0^2 \approx 1.2321. The paper's own duality \mathbb{M}_{n,q^{-1}}(\lambda') = \mathbb{M}_{n,q}(\lambda) closes the gap: it is an exact identity, verified here over all partitions of n \leq 9 in exact arithmetic, so the Q > 1 results are the Q^{-1} < 1 results read on conjugate diagrams. Clause 2 at the aether therefore describes the columns of \lambda where the cited statement describes rows. Nothing is lost and nothing is approximated; only a transposition is needed.

Deformed precedents for clause 3, and what each would need (literature)

Two published routes reach a limit-shape and fluctuation theorem for a deformed Plancherel measure. Neither covers \mathbb{M}_{n,q}, and neither has had its hypotheses checked for it.

The Jack deformation. Replacing symmetric-group characters by Jack characters with parameter \alpha > 0 (\alpha = 1 recovers the classical case) gives a deformed Plancherel measure whose bulk has a deterministic limit shape and Gaussian fluctuations [dolega-feray2014, §1.1--§1.2], and the construction extends to a general measure P^\chi attached to a family of characters on partitions [dolega-sniady2018, §1.4--§1.7]. The tool that makes the argument run is that the structure constants of Jack characters are polynomial in the deformation parameter [dolega-feray2014, §1.5, §4]. The Jack parameter is a different deformation from q, so this is a template, not a proof: a q-analogue along this route would first need a polynomiality or degree bound on the structure constants of the characters that define \mathbb{M}_{n,q}.

Approximate factorization. Biane proves concentration for any normalized positive-definite function \psi on the symmetric group whose values on a permutation \rho of support size l are bounded by c_l N^{-l/2} and approximately factorize on disjointly supported permutations: the induced measure on Young diagrams concentrates, and character values satisfy |\chi^\lambda(\rho) - \psi(\rho)| \le K(\delta + N^{-1})^{1/4} N^{-l/2} [biane2000, Def. 1.3, Thms 1--2]. Here N is the size of the symmetric group, written q in the source; it is unrelated to the deformation parameter q of this block. Using this route would require exhibiting \mathbb{M}_{n,q} as the measure of such a \psi and checking both bounds, which has not been done.

What is still open

The transfer to w_\lambda^{(n)}(q) = \dim_q^2/[n]_q! is unestablished, and that family is still in production. Restating this block does not migrate plancherel-term-7-formulation, whose \Phi_k functional is defined against a \dim_q^2 family. The canonical numerator for \Phi_k is the Molien weight f^\lambda q^{-\kappa_\lambda}\dim_q(\lambda)/[n]_q!, with the self-normalised \dim_q^2/\sum_\mu \dim_q^2 kept as a labelled comparison arm; what remains is to migrate the functional onto it. The choice is not cosmetic: the same harness ranks three different distinguished knots at k = 3 under three of the candidate families.

Clause 3 remains conjectural, isolating two open problems: q-deformed Kerov–Vershik convergence, and the operator-algebra realisation of the limit.
prop:centered-hecke-variance-positive:
Proposition Centred Hecke transfer matrix has strictly positive variance for every q > 0. Let q > 0. Let z = q^3/(q^2+1) and \tilde\sigma_i := \sigma_i - z \cdot 1. The variance

  \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) \;:=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(\tilde\sigma_i^2)
  \;=\;
  (q - q^{-1}) z + 1 - z^2
  \;=\;
  \frac{q^4 + q^2 + 1}{(q^2+1)^2}

is strictly positive for every q > 0, attains its minimum 3/4 at q = 1 and only there, and tends to 1 at both ends. At q_0 it is 0.75270211325196540159.

At z = q^3/(q^2+1) the variance is a Wenzl weight. The closed form above equals

  y_{(3)} + y_{(2,1)}
  \;=\; \frac{[4]_q}{[2]_q^3} + \frac{1}{[2]_q^2},

identically in q, which is the isospin-triplet weight \mu_+. So \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) = \mu_+, and its value at q_0 is the same 0.7527 that sits 22.85\,\% above the interface ceiling z = 0.61268803714646525160. It is also the magnitude of the extreme eigenvalues of the Markov–Gram form on the bilinear pairing at q_0, \pm 0.75270211.

See Table: Centred Hecke variance at q_0. The variance is well-separated from zero.

Positivity on the Temperley–Lieb quotient. Algebraically, (q^4+q^2+1)/(q^2+1)^2 > 0 holds on all of q > 0 without any auxiliary threshold inequality. Moreover, at z = q^3/(q^2+1), \mathrm{tr}_M factors through the Temperley–Lieb algebra \mathrm{TL}_n(q) with loop parameter [2]_q = q + q^{-1} \geq 2, defining a positive tracial state for every real q > 0 by Jones's theorem (Markov-trace GNS embedding H_\infty(q)/\mathcal{N} \hookrightarrow L(\mathcal{H})). Consequently, \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) is the variance of a positive tracial state for every q > 0.
rem:centered-hecke-variance-positive-int: Remark Non-degeneracy of the q-CLT limit from positive centred variance. Significance for the q-CLT. The second free cumulant \kappa_2^{(q)} = \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) prevents q-Gaussian degeneration. This guarantees a non-degenerate q-CLT limit for every real q > 0, where the Markov trace at z = q^3/(q^2+1) is a positive state.

prf:centered-hecke-variance-positive:
Proof Proof: centred Hecke variance is strictly positive. Apply the Hecke quadratic relation \sigma_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 and the Markov property:

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i^2)
  = (q - q^{-1}) \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i) + 1
  = (q - q^{-1}) z + 1.

Hence

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\tilde\sigma_i^2)
  =
  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i^2 - 2 z \sigma_i + z^2)
  =
  (q - q^{-1}) z + 1 - 2 z^2 + z^2
  =
  (q - q^{-1}) z + 1 - z^2.

This is the variance. Both steps are convention-independent: they use only the quadratic relation and \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i) = z.

Closed form. Substituting z = q^3/(q^2+1) and q - q^{-1} = (q^2-1)/q:

  (q - q^{-1})\,z \;=\; \frac{q^2(q^2-1)}{q^2+1},
  \qquad
  z^2 \;=\; \frac{q^6}{(q^2+1)^2}.

Over the common denominator (q^2+1)^2,

  \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i)
  \;=\; \frac{q^2(q^2-1)(q^2+1) + (q^2+1)^2 - q^6}{(q^2+1)^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^6 - q^2 + q^4 + 2q^2 + 1 - q^6}{(q^2+1)^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^4 + q^2 + 1}{(q^2+1)^2}.

Positivity. Numerator and denominator are both strictly positive for every real q, so \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) > 0 unconditionally — no regime hypothesis is needed. For the sharp bound, set t = q^2 > 0 and write f(t) = (t^2+t+1)/(t+1)^2. Then

  f'(t) \;=\; \frac{t-1}{(t+1)^3},

which is negative on (0,1), zero at t = 1, and positive on (1,\infty). So f attains its global minimum at t = 1, i.e. q = 1, where f(1) = 3/4, and f(t) \to 1 as t \to 0^+ and as t \to \infty. Therefore

  \tfrac{3}{4} \;\leq\; \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) \;<\; 1
  \qquad \text{for all } q > 0,

with equality on the left only at q = 1. At q_0 the value is 0.75270211325196540159. \square

Identification. The closed form is not a new quantity. Since [2]_q = (q^2+1)/q and [4]_q = [2]_q(q^2+q^{-2}),

  \frac{[4]_q}{[2]_q^3} + \frac{1}{[2]_q^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^4+1}{(q^2+1)^2} + \frac{q^2}{(q^2+1)^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^4+q^2+1}{(q^2+1)^2},

so \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) = y_{(3)} + y_{(2,1)} = \mu_+ identically in q — the centred second moment of a single Hecke generator is the isospin-triplet Wenzl weight.
rem:archimedean-macroscopic-washout:
Remark Archimedean macroscopic wash-out: why bounded observers see continuous q-Gaussian bell curves on a discrete aether. Origin of continuous distributions. Macroscopic observers measure auto-correlated sums \mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{macro}}(\Phi) = n^{-1} \sum \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_{j_i}(\Phi)). By the q-CLT, the rescaled sum converges to a q-Gaussian G_{q_0}(t, x) peaked at \mathrm{tr}_M(\Phi) with width \sqrt{\kappa_2^{(q)}/n}.

q-Gaussian rather than Gaussian. Braid relations impose global correlations. Systems with global correlations possess q-Gaussian attractors [marsh2006]. At q_0 \approx 1.110, the width deviates from a Gaussian. The probabilistic macroscopic behavior emerges as the CLT attractor.
prop:brane-tower-q-laplacian-decay:
Proposition Brane-tower convergence: q-Laplacian exponential decay drives the \hbar_q^{2n} tail bound. Summing over the brane tower yields the infinite jet prolongation

  T(\rho) \;=\; \sum_{n \geq 1} \hbar_q^{2n} \, \Delta^{(n)}(\rho).

The tower sum converges absolutely. It is dominated by the local contribution.

Bound. For 1 < q < q_*, where q_* \approx 1.2 is the edge of the range on which the proof's geometric series converges (this range contains q_0 \approx 1.110), and bounded L^2 norm:

  \boxed{\;
  \bigl|\,T(\rho) - \hbar_q^2 \,\Delta^{(1)}(\rho)\,\bigr|
  \;\leq\;
  \hbar_q^4 \, \|\rho\|_{L^2} \cdot
    \frac{q^{-2}}{1 - q^{-2}}
  \;}

The remainder decays geometrically with ratio q^{-2} < 1.

Mechanism. High-wavenumber Reeb modes suffer exponential damping. For any fixed mode k, the prefactor \hbar_q^{2n} (with \hbar_q^2 \approx 0.0098 at q_0) outweighs the growth (\lambda_k^{(q)})^n of the iterated Laplacian as long as \hbar_q^2 \lambda_k^{(q)} < 1. The geometric series converges because q^{-2}\hbar_q^2 < 1.
rem:brane-tower-q-laplacian-decay-interp: Remark Physical reading: local domination of the brane-tower integration. Physical reading. Non-local integration restricts appreciable contributions to the lowest jet levels. The local single-jet contribution leads. Corrections form a geometric series.
prf:brane-tower-q-laplacian-decay:
Proof Proof of the brane-tower convergence bound. The absolute-convergence bound follows by direct geometric-series estimation on the iterated Laplacian.

Step 1: q-integer asymptotic. For q > 1, the q-integer [k]_q = (q^k - q^{-k})/(q - q^{-1}) satisfies

  [k]_q \;=\; \frac{q^k}{q - q^{-1}}\,\bigl(1 - q^{-2k}\bigr)
  \;\leq\;
  \frac{q^k}{q - q^{-1}}.

Squaring and applying \hbar_q = (q - 1)/q gives \lambda_k^{(q)} = [k]_q^2 \hbar_q / L_q^2 \leq C\,q^{2k} for a constant C = \hbar_q / \bigl((q - q^{-1})^2 L_q^2\bigr).

Step 2: Single-jet bound. The \hbar_q^2 \Delta^{(1)} term on a normalised mode e_k of the Reeb bundle yields

  \bigl|\langle e_k, \hbar_q^2 \Delta^{(1)} e_k \rangle\bigr|
  \;=\;
  \hbar_q^2 \, \lambda_k^{(q)}
  \;\leq\;
  \hbar_q^2 \cdot C \, q^{2k}.

For the leading mode k = 1, this quantity is finite. Higher modes produce exponentially suppressed corrections, controlled in Step 4.

Step 3: Iterated-Laplacian bound. The n-th iteration \Delta^{(n)} on the same mode yields

  \bigl|\langle e_k, \Delta^{(n)} e_k\rangle\bigr|
  \;=\;
  (\lambda_k^{(q)})^n
  \;\leq\;
  C^n \, q^{2nk}.

Thus, the \hbar_q^{2n} tower coefficient on mode k is at most

  \hbar_q^{2n} \cdot C^n \, q^{2nk}
  \;=\;
  \bigl(\hbar_q^2 \, C \, q^{2k}\bigr)^n.

Step 4: Geometric-series sum. Sum over n with k = 1 fixed to extract the dominant mode contribution. Use \hbar_q^2 C q^2 < 1, which holds for q \in (1, q_*) with q_* \approx 1.2. This range comfortably covers the aether q_0 \approx 1.110:

  \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \hbar_q^{2n} C^n q^{2n}
  \;=\;
  \frac{\hbar_q^2 \, C \, q^2}{1 - \hbar_q^2 \, C \, q^2}
  \;<\;\infty.

Step 5: Leading versus remainder. Separate the n = 1 term:

  T(\rho) - \hbar_q^2 \,\Delta^{(1)}(\rho)
  \;=\;
  \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \hbar_q^{2n} \, \Delta^{(n)}(\rho).

On the leading mode Step 3 is an equality, \langle e_1, \Delta^{(n)} e_1\rangle = \lambda_1^n with \lambda_1 = \lambda_1^{(q)} = \hbar_q / L_q^2. The uniform bound on \Delta^{(n)} makes \lambda_1^n bounded in n, and a bounded sequence of powers has \lambda_1 \leq 1. Therefore

  \bigl| T(\rho) - \hbar_q^2 \,\Delta^{(1)}(\rho) \bigr|
  \;\leq\;
  \|\rho\|_{L^2}
  \cdot
  \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \hbar_q^{2n} \lambda_1^{n}
  \;\leq\;
  \|\rho\|_{L^2}
  \cdot
  \frac{\hbar_q^4}{1 - \hbar_q^2}.

Finally \frac{1}{1 - \hbar_q^2} \leq \frac{q^{-2}}{1 - q^{-2}} on 1 < q \leq q_*. With x = q^{-1} and \hbar_q = 1 - x, this reads 1 - x^2 \leq 2x^3 - x^4. The difference f(x) = 2x^3 - x^4 + x^2 - 1 has f'(x) = 2x(1 + 3x - 2x^2) > 0 on (0, 1] and f(1/1.2) > 0, so it holds on [1/1.2, 1]. This yields the displayed bound.

Direct eigenvalue bound. Bounding the tail directly through the exact leading eigenvalue avoids absorbing the Step-1 constant C into C q^2 \leq q^{-2} (which would require L_q \geq q^2 \sqrt{\hbar_q}/(q - q^{-1}) \approx 1.855 rather than the normalized value L_q = \sqrt{\hbar_q}), and therefore requires no auxiliary condition on L_q beyond the uniform bound.

Sharpness. At q_0 \approx 1.110, \hbar_q \approx 0.099 and q^{-2} \approx 0.812. Therefore, the geometric ratio q^{-2} \hbar_q^2 \approx 0.008 \ll 1. sec:molecular-hecke-algebra-intro: This section extends the atomic constructor to multi-atom systems. The molecular braid joins pre-computed atomic braids inside a single Hecke algebra. Inter-atomic crossing coefficients record how strands from different nuclei interact. Two atoms share a single electron trefoil to form a covalent bond. The ILP characterisation of the covalent bond identifies that shared trefoil as the inverse trefoil T_{2,3}^{-1}, the minimum-crossing knot operator with positive binding energy. With these four objects in hand, molecules are computed by Hopf-linking atoms. Unlike synthetic topological stereochemistry — where macroscopic molecular backbones are themselves tied into trefoil knots and catenanes in three-dimensional space, beginning with the synthetic molecular trefoil knot of Christiane O. Dietrich-Buchecker and Jean-Pierre Sauvage [dietrich-buchecker-sauvage1989] and classified via spatial graph chirality by Erica Flapan [flapan2000] — the braids here live in the internal Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_n(q) of the constituent nucleons and shared electrons, modelling ordinary covalent bonds rather than mechanically interlocked macrocycles.
def:molecular-braid:
Definition Molecular braid H_{N_{\mathrm{mol}}}(q). Let \mathcal{A}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{A}_k be pre-computed atomic braids with strand counts n_i = A_i + Z_i. The molecular braid is the element

  \mathcal{M}(A_1, \ldots, A_k; \mathcal{B}) \;\in\; H_{N_{\mathrm{mol}}}(q), \qquad N_{\mathrm{mol}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i

constructed iteratively as follows:

  1. Atomic assembly. Embed each atomic braid \mathcal{A}_i \in H_{n_i}(q) into H_{N_{\mathrm{mol}}}(q) using the standard inclusion \iota_i that shifts generator indices.
  2. Inter-atomic crossings. For each pair of atoms (i, j) with i < j, apply the inter-atomic crossing operators determined by the molecular crossing table.
  3. Shared-electron Hopf linking. For each covalent bond b \in \mathcal{B} connecting atoms i and j with bond order k_b, select k_b electron trefoils from atom i and Hopf-link them to atom j.
  4. Iterative reduction. After each assembly step, apply Gröbner–Shirshov reduction to normal form before proceeding to the next step.

Equivalently, \mathcal{M} = \mathrm{NF}\bigl(\prod_i \iota_i(\mathcal{A}_i) \cdot \prod_{i<j} C_{\mathrm{mol}} \cdot \prod_b L_b\bigr).

The binding energy of the molecule relative to its constituent atoms is

  \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}} = \alpha \left( \sum_{i=1}^{k} \Phi_1(\mathcal{A}_i) - \Phi_1(\mathcal{M}) \right)

where \alpha = m_e \times 8G is the atomic mass formula scale.
rem:molecular-braid-remark: Remark Sign of the molecular binding energy. Positive \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}} means the molecule is bound relative to its constituent atoms.
rem:molecular-crossing-table:
Remark Inter-atomic crossing coefficients. The atomic crossing table governs intra-atomic interactions (strong + EM). For inter-atomic crossings, only electromagnetic interactions remain — the strong force is confined within each nucleus. The inter-atomic crossing coefficients are:

See Table.

where subscripts i, j denote atoms, not strands. Key differences from the intra-atomic table:

  • \mathfrak{p}_i\mathfrak{p}_j is purely electromagnetic (\sigma, repulsive) — the strong \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p} crossing only operates within the same nucleus.
  • \mathfrak{n}_i\mathfrak{n}_j and \mathfrak{p}_i\mathfrak{n}_j are identity — neutrons from different atoms do not interact electromagnetically.
  • \mathfrak{p}_ie_j retains the EM attraction — this is the covalent bond channel. An electron from atom j attracted to proton i creates the shared-electron Hopf link.

The transfer matrix for inter-atomic crossing \sigma_g between strands s (atom i) and t (atom j) is:

  T_{st}^{\mathrm{inter}} =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    c_{st} q + d_{st} & c_{st}(q - q^{-1}) \\
    c_{st} & c_{st} q^{-1} + d_{st}
  \end{pmatrix}

using the (c, d) coefficients from the table above. For identity crossings (c = 0, d = 1), T_{st}^{\mathrm{inter}} reduces to the 2 \times 2 identity matrix — the strand passes through without generating a Hecke generator.

def:covalent-bond-shared-trefoil:
Definition Covalent bond as shared electrons. A covalent bond of order k between atoms i and j is the Hopf linking of k electrons across the two nuclei. Specifically, let e_1, \ldots, e_k be electrons from atom i. Each electron is the word \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 in its local H_3(q), whose closure is the Hopf link.

In the molecular braid, the covalent bond operator for bond b connecting atoms i and j is:

  L_b = \prod_{e=1}^{k_b} \sigma_{g_e(\mathfrak{p}_j)}^{-1} \cdot \sigma_{g_e(\mathfrak{p}_i)}^{-1}

where g_e(\mathfrak{p}_j) is the generator index for the crossing between shared electron e and proton \mathfrak{p}_j of atom j. Both crossings are \sigma^{-1} (EM attraction), so each shared electron contributes two attractive crossings—one to each nucleus.

Remark Covalent bond orders and LP-dual electron assignment. A bond of order k contributes 2k attractive crossings. The LP dual finds the optimal assignment of electrons to bonding positions by minimizing the total \Phi_1.

Bond orders correspond directly to shared pairs:

  • k = 1: single bond (H-H, C-H, C-C), 1 shared pair.
  • k = 2: double bond (C=O, C=C), 2 shared pairs.
  • k = 3: triple bond (C\equivO, N\equivN), 3 shared pairs.
prop:ilp-covalent-bond:
Proposition The H_2 bond word among the powers of V_s is V_s^3. The covalent bond word is selected by the same rule as every other canonical word: \gamma\gamma construction followed by reading-3 confinement. Write V_s = \sigma_s \sigma_{s+1}^{-1} for the pair-production unit. The H_2 word lives on twelve strands: each atom is a nucleon word V^m and an electron word V^k on its own three-strand windows, and a bond letter K sits at a junction site s \in \{4, 5\} between the two atoms. Reading 3 asks \chi_\lambda \geq 0 on every block with y_\lambda > 0 at z = q^3/(q^2+1), at every level 1, \dots, 12.

Proposition. Let the nucleon be V^m with m \in \{3, 6\} and the electron V^k with k \in \{0, 3, 6\}, the powers that pass reading 3 on their own three strands. At the proton-anchored q = q_0 \approx 1.10998, among the bond letters restricted to the powers K \in \{V_s, V_s^2, V_s^3\} at s \in \{4, 5\}, the bonded H_2 word passes reading 3 exactly for K = V_s^3, at either site. The uniqueness is a statement about this family of powers only; it does not hold for the full term alphabet of the photon (see the remark below).

Why the inverse trefoil is excluded

An earlier selection took the minimum-crossing knot from a list of knots and obtained the inverse trefoil T_{2,3}^{-1} = \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1}. Every \gamma\gamma word has even length, since each vertex contributes two letters, and the inverse trefoil has three. So it is not a \gamma\gamma word and cannot be the bond word under the one rule.

Scope

The result is a finite computation at a single value of q, the proton-anchored q_0, where every character is evaluated in 40-digit arithmetic. No other value of q is tested, and q_0 is fixed by calibration, so the proposition is a statement about that one point. The computation covers nucleon powers m \leq 6, electron powers k \leq 7, bond powers at most 3, the configuration with no proton–electron letter and no junction letter, both atom orders. Bond powers above 3 are not tested.

The hypothesis on the electron carries the uniqueness. If the electron is a \gamma\gamma power that fails reading 3 on its own strands (k \in \{1, 2, 4, 5, 7\}), the bonded word can still pass with K = V_4 or K = V_4^2: the bond repairs a constituent that fails alone. Read with reading 3 applied to the bonded word only, the cheapest such state (m = 3, k = 1, K = V_4, 18 crossings) ties in crossing count with the cheapest V^3-bonded state (m = 3, k = 0, K = V_4^3). Whether the constituents of a bonded group must also pass alone is therefore part of the selection rule, not a consequence of it. The selection rule requires it: every particle must pass reading 3 on its own strands as well as inside the bonded word. Under that rule the hypothesis on the electron holds and K = V_s^3 is the unique bond. The same holds outside the \gamma\gamma electron grammar: with a stabilised torus electron T(2,m), the V_s and V_s^2 bonds also pass in some configurations. The proposition is stated only for electrons V^k, k \in \{0, 3, 6\}.

Remark: the electron \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 and the photon's term alphabet

The electron is now the word E = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \in B_3, whose closure is the Hopf link, and the photon is \gamma = 1 + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1}. Neither changes the proposition: with E in place of V^k, the powers V_s^k (k = 1, 2, 3) reproduce the rows above exactly, and only V_s^3 passes.

The photon, however, offers more bond letters than the powers of V_s. A photon absorbed at a junction window contributes one non-identity term of \gamma_s, so the letters at the windows s \in \{4, 5\} are \sigma_4, \sigma_5, \sigma_6, V_4, V_5. A computation fixed in advance tested every product of one, two or three of these letters, 155 bonds in all, each monomial on its own so that no value of \varphi is chosen. Its findings, at q_0 with nucleons V^3 and V^6 and both atom orders:

  1. The electron E passes reading 3 on its own strands, but only with equality: its character on the block (2,1) is 0 for every q, since \chi_{(2,1)}(\sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0) = -(q - q^{-1}) + (q - q^{-1}) = 0. The bare H_2 word passes.
  2. No single photon term that crosses the cut between the atoms passes. Of the 155 bonds, 37 pass in the order pe and 32 in the order ep; 30 and 25 of these cross the cut. So V_s^3 is not unique in the full alphabet.
  3. The passing cut-crossing bond with fewest crossings is \sigma_5^2: two photons, two crossings, a pure braid clasping the electron of the first atom to the first strand of the second. Its trace ratio is 1.12809, so the trace increases, while for V_s^3 it is 0.997 to 1.0.
  4. With the two-term trace, whose lepton insertion depends only on the total weight and the numbers of quark and lepton strands, the connected term vanishes on every word, so every result above is the same under the one-term and the two-term trace. This uses the strand charges Q = T^3 + 1/6 on quark strands and Q = T^3 - 1/2 on lepton strands, which are an assumption here.

The selection rule as it stands does not choose among the passing bonds. A rule by fewest crossings would select \sigma_5^2; a rule requiring the trace to fall would exclude it. Neither rule is part of the present selection, so the bond under the full photon alphabet is left open.

Trace

The Markov trace of the bonded word over the bare word is reported, not used for selection: 0.9984 to 0.9986 for every V^3 bond above. The binding energy formerly quoted for H_2 was computed on the inverse trefoil word and does not carry over to the \gamma\gamma bond.
sec:molecular-assembly-projector-intro:
A molecule is a composite braid: k sub-units assembled into a single word in H_N(q). Before specialising to any one molecule, record the general algebraic structure that the assembly forces.

The k sub-units determine a strand-partition \lambda = (n_1,\dots,n_k) with \sum_i n_i = N. The assembly factors through the parabolic subalgebra H_\lambda(q) \hookrightarrow H_N(q). Every such factorisation carries canonical assembly projectors onto the Wedderburn blocks of H_N(q). Projection onto the symmetric block is delocalisation.

Three things must be kept distinct. Existence of the projector is pure algebra. Optimality is the physics, selected by the binding LP/SDP. Energetics is the binding energy, corresponding to the trace-weight gap between the selected block and the next configuration.
def:molecular-strand-partition:
Definition Molecular strand-partition \lambda of N strands. Let a molecule be assembled from k sub-units carrying strand counts n_1,\dots,n_k. The molecular strand-partition is the composition

  \lambda = (n_1,\dots,n_k), \qquad |\lambda| = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i = N,

which records how the N strands of the composite braid in H_N(q) are distributed among the sub-units. Write \ell(\lambda) = k for the number of sub-units.
rem:molecular-strand-partition-remark: Remark Strand-partitions are fixed by connectivity. The strand-partition is fixed by what is joined to what. For three acetylene units, the carbon strand-partition is \lambda = (2,2,2), with N = 6 and k = 3 (benzene as the assembly projector).
def:parabolic-hecke-subalgebra:
Definition Parabolic Hecke subalgebra H_\lambda(q) \hookrightarrow H_N(q). Let \lambda = (n_1,\dots,n_k) be a strand-partition with \sum_i n_i = N. The parabolic Hecke subalgebra is the tensor product

  H_\lambda(q) \;=\; H_{n_1}(q) \otimes \cdots \otimes H_{n_k}(q) \;\hookrightarrow\; H_N(q),

generated by the Hecke generators \sigma_j that act within a single sub-unit block. The omitted generators, those joining two blocks, are the cross-block generators.
rem:parabolic-hecke-subalgebra-remark: Remark Generator counts of the parabolic subalgebra. The cross-block generators are precisely the crossings created when the sub-units bond. Equivalently H_\lambda(q) is the q-deformation of the Young subgroup S_\lambda \subset S_N. Its intra-unit generator count is N - k. The bonding degrees of freedom number k-1. For benzene's \lambda = (2,2,2), there are 3 intra-unit generators and 2 bonding generators linking the three units into a ring, with the third join closing the ring.
def:molecular-assembly-projector: Definition Molecular assembly projector e_{\lambda,\mu}. Let \lambda be a strand-partition of N and \mu \vdash N a Wedderburn block of H_N(q). The assembly projector e_{\lambda,\mu} \in H_N(q) is the canonical idempotent projecting the composite's module onto the irreducible block \mu. The distinguished case \mu = (N), projection onto the one-row symmetric block, is called delocalisation.
rem:molecular-assembly-projector-remark: Remark The assembly projector as a q-Young symmetriser. The assembly projector e_{\lambda,\mu} is the q-Young symmetriser for the pair (\lambda,\mu). Benzene is the case e_{(2,2,2),(6)} (benzene as the assembly projector), whose symmetric block is realised geometrically as the T(2,6) threading link.
